title: Council finalizes 2024–2027 multi-year budget
subtitle: Staffing phase-in, transit signs, hospital funding, housing reserve cut, bicentennial funding, and new direction on trails and streetscaping.
overview: Council met in a special budget session and finished the 2024–2027 multi-year budget in one day. Early administrative amendments lowered the starting 2024 increase, and further amendments brought the total levy increase to about 8.52 per cent, as stated by staff in the meeting. The mayor said the city portion was roughly in line with inflation and that the mayor would waive the time available under strong-mayor powers to veto, signing off the same day.

The biggest changes phased in permanent staffing over two years {{vote:m11}}, delayed some library costs {{vote:m12}}, cut the digital transit signs project {{vote:m14}}, and reduced the transfer to the Affordable Housing Reserve {{vote:m21}}. Council kept the full bicentennial funding after two cut proposals failed, and retained the 2024 hospital payment but funded it from a reserve {{vote:m19}}.

Council added money for physician recruitment, value-for-money reviews and health supports for encampments, and asked staff to study help for low-income homeowners with property tax penalties. Council also withdrew a proposal to stretch out transit expansion. In closed session, council received information on Farmers Market contractual obligations and gave staff direction.

decisions.detail: Council agreed to budget 50 per cent of permanent staffing resources in the first year and the rest in the second, lowering the 2024 amount {{vote:m11}}.
Council eliminated later-year capital funding and operating impacts for the digital signs project, so signs go ahead only at the already-approved hubs {{vote:m14}}.
Council reduced the 2024 transfer to the Affordable Housing Reserve by $400,000 {{vote:m21}}, after a proposal to increase it by $1,000,000 was defeated {{vote:m9}}.
Council funded the 2024 hospital installment of $750,000 from the tax rate contingency reserve {{vote:m19}}, rejecting a proposal to defer it to 2025 {{vote:m18}}.
Council shifted library budget amounts between years to phase in building maintenance positions for the new library {{vote:m12}}.

Council approved a two-year grant to the Guelph-Wellington Ontario Health Team for physician recruitment, conditional on County and Chamber of Commerce contributions and funded from a reserve {{vote:m8}}.
Council set aside $100,000 from the contingency reserve for health and safety supports tied to County-led wellness checks at encampments, with a report due by June 2024 {{vote:m13}}.
Council allocated up to $10,000 to study a needs-based program waiving penalties and suspending interest for low-income homeowners, reporting back by Q2 2024 {{vote:m20}}.

debate: On the staffing phase-in, supporters described it as a way to give relief in 2024 without cutting programs, and staff said they could support it. One councillor warned against slowing transit growth, though the chair noted the motion was about staffing costs.

On the digital signs, supporters said the project's cost had grown and the cut would not reduce bus service. Transit staff said customers without data, such as affordable pass users, seniors and newcomers, would be affected most, and said about 50 stops would be a reasonable start.

On the Affordable Housing Reserve, supporters of the cut said provincial Bill 23 now covers development charges on affordable units, no projects had approached the city, and funds could come from surplus if a project arose. Opponents said the reserve gives seed money to leverage other funding and that cutting it sends a poor message.

On the hospital payment, councillors opposed deferral because the hospital had only said it could live with a delay and the cost would land in later years. Finance staff cautioned that reserves were below target, and a councillor raised concerns about projected reserve shortfalls.

On the bicentennial, supporters of cuts said the city should limit costs in a tight year. Opponents said the funding leverages community investment, supports reconciliation work, and could be revisited once staff return with a plan. Staff did not support the cuts, and both proposals failed.
